Blue arrows labeled I show conventional current moving clockwise: rightward across the top, downward on the right, and leftward across the bottom. Black arrows and e⁻ labels show electrons moving in the opposite direction around the loop.

semantic_layer.text: Electrical current (I) is the rate of flow of positive charge.

semantic_layer.text: A steady current of 2.5 A is created in a wire for 1.0 minute. How much charge passed by any given point, and how many electrons would this be?

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: I equals Q divided by delta t, which leads to I equals 2.5 coulombs per second, equal to Q divided by t.
Q equals I times t, equal to 2.5 coulombs per second times 60 seconds, equal to 150 coulombs.
N equals 150 coulombs times one electron per 1.60 times 10 to the negative 19 coulombs, equal to 9.4 times 10 to the 20 electrons.
n equals 9.4 times 10 to the 20 electrons times one divided by 6.022 times 10 to the 23 electrons per mole, equal to 0.0016 mole.

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: A closed rectangular circuit contains a battery labeled V on the lower left and a zigzag resistor labeled R on the right. Multiple e-minus labels and arrowheads around the wire indicate electron motion: rightward along the bottom, upward on the right, leftward along the top, and downward on the left, forming a counterclockwise path.
semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Circuit with a battery V, resistor R, and counterclockwise electron-flow arrows.
A resistor labeled R is drawn as a zigzag circuit symbol, with an arrow and the words “circuit symbol” identifying it.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Omega equals ohm.
The units of ohms equal volts per ampere, equal joules per coulomb divided by coulombs per second.

semantic_layer.text: A resistor resists the flow of current.
They're often used to limit current in a part of a circuit. Wires themselves have some resistance, but we'll usually ignore it.

warnings.message: The handwritten annotation reads “Greek Omiga,” likely a misspelling of “Greek Omega.”

Sketch of a cylindrical resistor or wire carrying current I to the right. Its cross-sectional area is labeled A and its length is labeled L.

R equals rho times L divided by A.
The units of resistance, ohms, equal ohm-meters times meters divided by meters squared.

semantic_layer.text: (Superconductors — materials with zero resistance — are generally extremely low temperature. “High temperature” superconductors are those which exhibit R=0 above 77K, the boiling point of nitrogen.)

semantic_layer.text: Example  In the circuit below, is V higher at point A or B? What about I?

semantic_layer.text: We say that “voltage drops” across a resistor.
The current is the same at A and B!
The current is lower through this whole circuit due to the resistor.

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: A closed circuit is drawn as a traffic jam of small car-like boxes labeled “e⁻.” The boxes form a loop. A zigzag resistor labeled R interrupts the top of the loop, while a battery labeled V interrupts the bottom. The battery’s positive terminal is on the left and its negative terminal is on the right. semantic_layer.text: A flashlight bulb draws 300mA from its 1.5 V battery. What’s the resistance of the bulb? If the battery degrades and only produces 1.2 V how would the current change?

semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Sketch of a glowing flashlight with a bulb and two batteries inside.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Current equals voltage divided by resistance. Therefore, resistance equals voltage divided by current, which equals 1.5 volts divided by 0.30 amperes, or 5.0 ohms.
When the voltage decreases to 1.2 volts, current equals 1.2 volts divided by 5.0 ohms, which is 0.24 amperes, or 240 milliamperes.

semantic_layer.text: Suppose you want to connect your stereo to remote speakers. (a) If each wire must be 20 m long, what diameter copper wire should you use to keep the resistance less than 0.10 Ω per wire? (b) If the current to each speaker is 4.0 A, what is the potential difference, or voltage drop, across each wire?

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: A stereo receiver is connected to two remote speakers. Curved wire paths run from the receiver to each speaker, and each path is labeled 20 m.
semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Diagram of a stereo connected by 20 m wires to two remote speakers.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Part b. Voltage equals current times resistance, equal to 4.0 amperes times 0.10 ohm. The voltage across the resistance is 0.400 volt, or 400 millivolts. Annotations indicate amperes as coulombs per second and ohms as volts per ampere.

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: Hand-drawn series circuit. A voltage source V is at left with positive and negative terminals. Current I is shown clockwise around the loop. On the right, a resistor labeled R and WIRING is above a speaker symbol labeled SPEAKER.
semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Series-circuit sketch showing a voltage source, wire resistance, speaker, and clockwise current.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Part a. The resistivity of copper is 1.68 times 10 to the negative 8 ohm meters. The length is 20 meters, and the resistance is 0.10 ohm.

semantic_layer.normalized_math: A=\pi r^2=\pi\left(\frac d2\right)^2,\qquad R=\rho\frac LA=\frac{4\rho L}{\pi d^2}
semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Area equals pi r squared, equal to pi times d over 2 squared. Resistance equals resistivity times length over area, equal to 4 rho L over pi d squared.
d squared is greater than 4 rho L over pi R. Therefore, d is greater than the square root of 4 rho L over pi R. Substitution gives a diameter of 2.1 millimeters.
Power equals energy divided by time.
Electrical energy U equals charge q times voltage V.
Power equals charge times voltage divided by time, which equals current times voltage.
Power equals current times voltage.
The unit ampere equals coulombs per second.
The unit volt equals joules per coulomb.
The unit watt equals joules per second.
The unit ohm equals volts per ampere, which equals volt seconds per coulomb, which equals joule seconds per coulomb squared.
Watts equal amperes times volts, equal coulombs per second times joules per coulomb, equal joules per second.
Using V equals I R, power equals I times I R, which equals I squared R.
Using I equals V over R, power equals V over R times V, which equals V squared over R.
Power equals current times voltage.
Power equals current squared times resistance.
Power equals voltage squared divided by resistance.

V R M S equals the square root of the average of V naught squared sine squared of omega t, which equals the square root of V naught squared times one half, which equals V naught divided by the square root of two.
V R M S equals V naught divided by the square root of two.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: I equals V over R, which implies I equals V sub zero over R times sine of omega t.
I equals I sub zero times sine of omega t, where I sub zero equals V sub zero over R and is the peak current.
I R M S equals one over the square root of two times I sub zero.
Average power equals R M S current times R M S voltage.
Average power equals R M S current squared times resistance.
Average power equals R M S voltage squared divided by resistance.
